data.hypothesis: The catalog has three distinct, valid SIMD-scan programs and no repeats, but none beat the 49.62 µs baseline: the 16-byte scan measured 60.43 µs, the selected lane-bisection parent 77.82 µs, and the 64-byte variant 81.00 µs. This contrasting SIMD-prefix/scalar-remainder hybrid tests whether repeatedly restarting SIMD scans and locating a lane after each decoded code point costs more than it saves. It skips only complete 16-byte ASCII vectors; on the first vector containing any high bit, it sends the suffix from that block boundary to the strict scalar decoder. This avoids assuming the high-bit byte is a lead and preserves bounded loads, but gives up SIMD scanning of later ASCII runs. Measure it on the official mixed-width n=65536 workload; do not infer a speedup from synthetic inputs.

memory_lessons.applicability: The measured T2 SIMD variants motivate testing fallback frequency rather than just changing vector width or lane-location method.
memory_lessons.claim: The baseline measured 49.62 µs; the 16-byte SIMD scan, lane-bisection variant, and 64-byte scan measured 60.43, 77.82, and 81.00 µs respectively. All were valid on recorded correctness cases, but none established a speed benefit. The catalog reported three distinct programs and no repeated programs.
memory_lessons.next_experiment: Measure a SIMD-prefix/scalar-remainder variant on the official mixed-width workload and the official ASCII/malformed boundary cases.

data.notes: This is a distinct SIMD-prefix/scalar-remainder hybrid, not T1 whole-buffer SIMD validation. No commands or tests were run here; correctness and official-workload performance remain for the controller to evaluate. Prior measurements are observations, not a claim about this candidate.
transformations: Replaced repeated SIMD scans interleaved with scalar code-point decoding with a bounded SIMD prefix scan over complete 16-byte blocks.

On the first vector with high-bit bytes, call the strict scalar validator on the suffix beginning at that vector's known code-point boundary; the scalar decoder validates any leading ASCII and treats the first high-bit byte as input to validate.
Retained scalar tail handling, UTF-8 validity rules, run ABI, output, and thread budget.
